title: Refit a sink trap's J-bend onto both pipes, hand-tight
instruction: Refit the J-bend under the sink: fit it onto the tailpiece and the trap arm, then tighten both slip nuts by hand.
context: Clearing a clogged sink means taking the P-trap's J-bend off, clearing it and refitting it under the basin, inside the vanity: one of the commonest plumbing jobs. Plumbers (O*NET 47-2152.00: "Maintain or repair plumbing by replacing defective washers, replacing or mending broken pipes, or opening clogged drains") and general maintenance and repair workers (49-9071.00, about 1.5 million in the US: "Assemble, install, or repair ... pipe systems, plumbing") do it by hand in homes, apartments, hotels and offices. Refitting is the hard half: one rigid part goes onto two fixed pipes 88 mm apart at once, their ends hidden inside its legs; the first joint has to stay seated, undisturbed, while the second is made; and each slip nut is run four turns onto its thread square, without cross-threading. A loose trap leaks into the cabinet.
setup: Dream Labs' YAM station (scene=station), both arms at their ready pose. World frame: origin between the arm bases, x forward, y left, z up; the table top (z = 0.7475 m) is the floor of a bathroom vanity cabinet, and heights below are above it. Fixed: the back wall (painted drywall) at x = 0.58 m; the cabinet's sides (18 mm melamine) at y = +-0.47 m; the vanity top (30 mm laminate) 0.73 m up, with an undermount vitreous china basin (bowl 0.38 m across, 0.15 m deep) whose drain's underside is 0.56 m up. Fixed pipes, all 1-1/2 in tubular (38.1 mm outside): the drain's chrome-plated brass tailpiece, hanging straight down from the drain at (0.36, -0.045) m to its open end 0.330 m up; the white PVC trap arm, out of the wall's trap adapter 0.44 m up, running 0.175 m toward the arms and turning down (45 mm bend radius) on (0.36, 0.043) m to its open end 0.310 m up. On each pipe its slip nut (white PVC, 1-1/2 in, 11-1/2 threads per inch, 62 mm across, 68 mm across its four wings, 25 mm tall, 30 g), its beveled washer inside, slid up: the tailpiece's nut's bottom 0.400 m up, the trap arm's 0.365 m up. Loose: the J-bend (white PVC, 1-1/2 in, 140 g; legs 87.6 mm apart on centre with 41.4 mm bores and 47 mm threaded ends, 8.8 mm of thread; the inlet leg 125 mm and the outlet leg 100 mm tall from the bend's bottom), lying on its side on the cabinet floor with its legs toward the back wall, the inlet leg's axis along x at y = 0.135 m and the bend's bottom at x = 0.185 m, the outlet leg to its left. Refitted, the J-bend's bottom is 0.235 m up, the tailpiece 30 mm into the inlet leg and the trap arm 25 mm into the outlet leg. The parts are a standard trap kit (e.g. Oatey HDC9682) and a pop-up drain's tailpiece; for a real trial the drain and the trap adapter can be fixed to a plywood mock-up at these heights. Friction 0.9. The layout is fixed (-E object_jitter=0).
scoring: Seated, 0.2: the J-bend on both pipes at once, each pipe at least 10 mm inside its leg (a pencil line 10 mm from each pipe's end is hidden inside the leg) and coaxial with it within 3 mm, the J-bend upright within 5 degrees. For each slip nut (tailpiece, trap arm): started, 0.15: run at least one full turn (2.2 mm) onto its leg's thread (a paint ring 2 mm below the thread's top is hidden under the nut); snug, 0.15 more: run on its four turns, its washer squeezed home (no thread shows below the nut, and it will not turn further by hand). Hanging, 0.2: seated with both nuts snug and nothing holding the J-bend but its nuts (no gripper within 10 mm of the J-bend or a nut, the J-bend not moving more than 2 mm), held 1 s. A nut cannot start on a leg that is not on its pipe and coaxial with it (within 2 mm and 3 degrees); pushed down there it stops on the thread's start and scores nothing. Score = the sum at the end of the trial; the trial ends as a success once hanging holds.
reset_notes: In simulation nothing is consumed. Real trials: unscrew both slip nuts and slide them up to their tape marks on the pipes, take the J-bend off and lay it on its marked place on the cabinet floor. No water is used. PVC threads wear slowly: replace the J-bend and nuts (a kit costs about $10) when a nut no longer runs on freely.
fidelity: Pipes, J-bend and nuts are rigid, at real size; pipes slide into the legs (1.6 mm clearance). As our pipes are rigid, a force of at most 15 N stands in for a leg mouth's bevel and real pipes' play: it centres a leg pushed onto a pipe end within 4 mm of its axis; further off, it does not go on. Threads are our model: a nut starts only on a leg on its pipe and aligned (2 mm, 3 deg), then turns only with a gripping hand swinging round its axis, 2.2 mm a turn, snug after 4. Washers are in the nuts.
